wgpu_mc.notice.restart_pending: Restart Minecraft to apply the marked settings
wgpu_mc.notice.restart_applied: Restart Minecraft for these settings to take effect
wgpu_mc.option.frames_in_flight.tooltip: How many frames the CPU may record ahead of the GPU. One is a full stall on every frame, two hides the recording behind the GPU, three adds a frame of latency for a little more slack.
wgpu_mc.option.animated_textures.tooltip: Whether the block textures Minecraft animates move: fire, lava, the campfire, the sea lantern, every sprite with an .mcmeta that says so. Fancy draws those faces from the game's own block atlas, which the game is animating frame by frame, so they move exactly as they do in vanilla and nothing is copied. Fast draws them from this renderer's own copy of the sprite, which is a single frame - the picture this renderer drew before the animated-texture path existed. It also covers the two places fire is drawn by Minecraft rather than by us - the first-person burning overlay and the flames on a burning entity - which are held still on the frame they were on rather than drawn differently. It is a fidelity choice rather than a speed one, and switching it takes effect after the block models are baked again: a second or two, then the loaded sections are meshed again.
wgpu_mc.option.dump_frames.tooltip: Write out the next N frames the renderer presents, as raw files under wgpu-frames, and zero for none. A dump is about the frame that is on screen, and one frame rarely settles a flicker: a handful in a row is what says whether what you are looking at is there on every frame or on every other one. Turning it to zero and up again asks for another handful.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain.tooltip: Draw the terrain from the meshes the Rust baker builds, in the pass Minecraft's own solid layer would have used. That pass is the game's opaque section-layer group, so the cutout layer is drawn from the same meshes too - it is the same render pass. The translucent layer, the entities and everything else drawn afterwards stay Minecraft's, against the depth this fills. Off is Minecraft's own terrain. Turning it on asks Minecraft to rebuild its sections, so it takes a second or so to show.
wgpu_mc.option.host_validation.tooltip: Load the graphics backend's own validation layer: D3D12's debug layer, Vulkan's validation layer, or GL's debug output. It is written by the graphics vendor rather than by wgpu, reports through the driver's debug output, and catches what wgpu cannot see - a barrier in the wrong place, a resource used before its GPU work finished, a descriptor the driver disagrees about. It was unconditional here, so every player loaded a vendor debug layer they were not reading; it is off by default now. GPU-based validation needs it. This does NOT switch wgpu's own validation on or off: wgpu checks every call it is given whatever this says, which is what lets an error name the call it came from, so turning this off does not make an invalid call silent - it removes the vendor's second opinion and its debug output. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch.
wgpu_mc.option.shader_debug_info.tooltip: Build the wgpu instance with its DEBUG flag: debug information in shaders and objects. This validates nothing and costs nothing per draw. What it decides is whether the objects this renderer creates carry the information a graphics debugger reads - RenderDoc, Nsight, PIX, spirv-dis - so a capture with it off names things like texture_47 instead of wgpu-mc block atlas. On by default; turn it off only if a driver is measurably slowed by the extra metadata. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch. WGPU_DEBUG=0 overrides it from outside the game.
wgpu_mc.option.validate_indirect_calls.t: Check the arguments in an indirect draw buffer before issuing the draw, and turn the draw into a no-op when they are out of bounds: an index range that does not fit the bound index buffer, an instance range that does not fit an instance-stepped vertex buffer, and a non-zero first instance on a device without indirect-first-instance support. On by default and it should stay on: without it an out-of-bounds indirect argument is undefined behaviour rather than an error, and on D3D12 the built-in instance index stops accounting for first instance at all - which would draw terrain from the wrong offsets rather than fail. What it costs is a bounds check on a handful of integers per indirect call, not per drawn section. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch. WGPU_VALIDATION_INDIRECT_CALL=0 overrides it from outside the game.
wgpu_mc.option.discard_backend_labels.to: Do not pass the labels this renderer gives its objects down to the graphics backend. Every buffer, texture, pipeline and bind group here is named, and a name is a string lookup and a driver call each time one is created - measurable in a world that allocates as it loads, and not measurable at all once it has settled. Off by default, because what the names buy is that a driver's own validation error and a graphics debugger both say wgpu-mc section arena instead of a handle, which is most of what makes either readable. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch. WGPU_DISCARD_HAL_LABELS=1 overrides it from outside the game.
wgpu_mc.option.allow_noncompliant_adapte: Allow wgpu to offer an adapter whose driver does not meet the graphics API's own requirements - in practice a Vulkan driver reporting a major compliance version of 0, which wgpu otherwise refuses to use at all. Off by default, because the point of the requirement is that such a driver may be broken in ways wgpu cannot see: it is an escape hatch for a machine where nothing else is offered, not a setting to leave on. With it off and no compliant adapter, the renderer reports that it could not create one and the game shows its no-supported-backend screen. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch. WGPU_ALLOW_UNDERLYING_NONCOMPLIANT_ADAPTER=1 overrides it from outside the game.
wgpu_mc.option.gpu_based_validation.tool: Ask the backend's validation layer to check what the GPU is actually asked to do, rather than only the commands that were recorded: the same vendor layer as Host validation, but running on the GPU. That is what catches a mistake only the hardware can see - a read of a resource whose earlier write has not landed, a shader reading past a binding, a missing barrier between two passes. It is the slowest thing here by a wide margin and it is a development tool, so it is off by default. It needs Host validation, because it is that same layer doing more; asking for this alone turns that on with it rather than doing nothing. The wgpu instance is created with this flag, so switching takes effect on the next launch.
wgpu_mc.option.diagnostics.tooltip: Write the renderer's dumps out as files: the frame the game is showing, the textures it is showing it with, and a sprite atlas after the frame or two it takes Minecraft to compose one. The dump itself is asked for by a wgpu-dump-now file in the run directory, because a dump is about one specific frame; this is the switch that lets the ask through, and wgpu-dump-frames turns both it and the logging on. What the renderer says while it does it is the Logging switch above, so a diagnostic session is usually both.
wgpu_mc.option.logging.tooltip: Write the renderer's diagnostic log lines: each pipeline the first time it is used, the binding plan it resolves names against, each render pass with its draw count, the draw and submission counters once a second, the sprite-animation pass counter, and the reports for the uploads and uniforms the renderer verifies as it goes. Off by default, because it is a line per pipeline on top of a line per second. It is a log switch and not a dump switch: Diagnostics above is what writes the frame and texture files, so either can be on without the other. This is the wgpu-logging marker as a switch, and the wgpu_mc.diagnostics system property or WGPU_MC_DIAGNOSTICS environment variable still turns it on from outside the game.
wgpu_mc.option.binding_verbosity.tooltip: Log how every binding name was resolved against a pipeline's binding plan, and what the plan was left holding: a name that only matched through the shader shim's _wm_texshim / _wm_sampler suffix, the names a plan can be bound under when one of them is not in it, and the slots a pipeline change left empty. This is the detailed version of the warning the renderer always prints when a binding is not in the plan at all, and it is the switch to turn on when a shader reads nothing and the question is which name it was looking for. This is the wgpu-binding-log marker as a switch.
wgpu_mc.option.section_timing.tooltip: Time the section feed, phase by phase, and report the averages. What the feed does is what runs on Minecraft's chunk-build threads - looking up the light of the sections around a rebuild, reading the block data out of the container, and handing the lot to the native side in one call - so this is the switch that answers "what does one section rebuild cost, and which part of it" with three numbers instead of a guess. The averages appear on the F3 screen while it is on. Off by default: it is a clock read per phase per section, and closing it costs nothing at all. This is the wgpu-section-timing marker as a switch.
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_base_mip_only: Atlas sampled from its base mip only
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_base_mip_only.toolt:
Sample the game's own block atlas from its base mip level only, so a distant animated sprite resolves to a single texel of it rather than a blend of mip levels.

Off, because the game animates the whole chain rather than one level of it: TextureAtlas#uploadAnimationFrames walks every level and renders the current frame of each animated sprite into each of them, through that level's own view and its own uniform buffer. No level is staler than any other, so there is no stale level for a clamp to avoid - and clamping to 0.0 does not make the animated textures fresher, it makes them alias: one texel of a 16x16 sprite per pixel is the temporal noise a mip chain exists to remove. It is a switch because the case for it is a picture rather than an argument, and a run with it on against a run with it off is what settles it. Applying it rebuilds the graph, because a sampler is built with the pipelines rather than per draw.
wgpu_mc.option.window_mode.tooltip:
How the window fills the screen.

Exclusive is GLFW's monitor mode - a real display mode switch, the same thing Minecraft's own Fullscreen does. Borderless covers the monitor with no decorations and does not change the display mode, which is what to pick if you alt-tab. Windowed is a window.

The setting is stored by the wgpu-mc renderer rather than in options.txt, because there are three of them and options.txt has one boolean - but it is applied the moment you pick it.
wgpu_mc.option.fullscreen_mode.tooltip:
How the window fills the screen.

Exclusive is GLFW's monitor mode - a real display mode switch, and what the game's own fullscreen has always been. Borderless covers the monitor with no decorations and does not change the display mode, which is what to pick if you alt-tab. Off is a window.

The game's own fullscreen key (F11 by default) toggles between Off and whichever mode is chosen here, so the key keeps working and this page decides what it returns to.

Takes effect as soon as it is applied: none of the three touches the device or the swapchain's format, so there is nothing to restart for.
wgpu_mc.option.game_atlas_blend_mips: Blend the game atlas' mip levels
wgpu_mc.option.game_atlas_blend_mips.too:
Whether the sampler for the game's own block atlas blends between two mip levels or picks one and writes it.

On - which is what the renderer ships, and what vanilla does (GL_LINEAR_MIPMAP_LINEAR) - blends them. Off picks one and writes it, which is sharper for a texture that holds still.

**It does not affect the shimmer on flowing water and lava**, which an earlier version of this text claimed: a player measured both settings and the lava shimmered under each. The blend only mixes two mip levels of one frame, so it cannot be the cause of anything that survives being turned off. Kept because the two differ for content that moves and which one a player prefers is a picture rather than an argument.

Takes effect on the next frame; applying it rebuilds the graph, and nothing is baked.
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_lod_bias.tooltip:
Shift the mip level the terrain shaders pick for the block atlases. 0 is no shift and the fetch a plain textureSample would make; positive samples a coarser level and negative a finer one, so a blurry picture that sharpens as this goes negative means the chosen level was too coarse, and one that never changes means the level was never the problem.

It is a measure rather than a picture setting. The level comes from the screen-space derivative of the texture coordinates, and every reading of this renderer's coordinates says that derivative should match the game's - so the number is here to disagree with the reading if the picture does.

Read per draw, so it takes effect on the next frame: nothing is baked and no pipeline is rebuilt. That is the point of it - the same value as a shader constant could not be told apart from one that never reached the GPU.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_occlusion.tooltip:
Honour the game's own occlusion graph - the list of sections LevelRenderer worked out are on screen - and skip the sections it did not name. On is the faster answer and, while that list is right, the correct one.

It is a switch because the list is a snapshot rather than a per-frame fact. LevelRenderer.applyFrustum is the only thing that refills it, and it runs only when the camera has turned by more than two degrees or the occlusion graph reports that something changed. Between those moments the list is whatever the last refill produced, so a section this side has baked and the game's list has not caught up with is skipped by the terrain pass - while the game's own mesh for it stays suppressed, because this side was told about it. A section neither side draws is a 16x16x16 hole, and it fills in the moment anything dirties it. With this off every section the frustum contains is drawn, which costs frame time and leaves no holes to attribute.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_no_cull.tooltip: Draw every pipeline the render graph builds without back-face culling, so the picture stops depending on the winding of a triangle at all. This is a diagnostic for a picture that is inside out: with both faces rasterized, "the winding is wrong" and "the depth test keeps the wrong end" stop looking the same, which is the only way to tell them apart. It is not a mode to play with - the second copy of every quad is shaded with the far side's lighting, and on a translucent quad the two copies land at the same depth, where which of them survives is not defined. It is read by every pipeline the graph builds and not only by the terrain one, because that is where the wgpu-terrain-no-cull marker it replaces was read; the name is the bug it was written for. Applying it rebuilds the graph's pipelines, because a cull mode is part of the pipeline rather than something a draw can change.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_greater_depth: Terrain with the depth test reversed
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_greater_depth.too: Draw every pipeline the render graph builds with the depth test the opposite way round, so the faces behind are the ones kept. The other half of the pair above: it is what "the depth values are the wrong way round" would look like, and the other reading of a picture whose front faces are missing. Depth writes are unchanged - the test is what moved - so the picture is the far side of everything the camera can see through, with the sky and the HUD drawn over it as usual. This is the wgpu-terrain-greater-depth marker as a switch, and it too applies to every pipeline the graph builds. Applying it rebuilds the graph's pipelines.
wgpu_mc.option.upload_report.tooltip: Report what the renderer's buffer uploads did: every mapped write into a constant buffer with the first integers it carried, whether the bytes actually arrived in the buffer - checked by reading them back from the GPU, so that report costs a copy and a map of its own - and the staging totals for those writes once a second. It is the switch to turn on when an upload is suspected of not landing: "mapped write to ... first 12 ints" and "the bytes written to ... did not arrive" are the two lines that tell a buffer that received the wrong bytes apart from one that received none. Off by default, and independent of the Logging switch above, because it is a line per upload and the readback is a copy per upload. This is the wgpu-upload-report marker as a switch.
